sources.text: The Blockade on Iran is Deepening – But Also Widening Other avenues are emerging as the U.S. continues its tight hold on shipping to Iran (CENTCOM) By The Maritime Executive 2026-10-23 18:06:20 It is generally accepted that the U.S. naval blockade on Iran, targeting both Iranian ships and ports, is nearly 100 percent effective. Iran has not been able to export oil for many weeks, and stocks built up as a contingency reserve before the war are now either exhausted or are nearly run down. The effect is now being felt by the Iranian government, which will be losing approximately 40 percent of the revenues on which its annual budget is based. U.S. Central Command highlighted on Thursday, October 22, that it was marking 100 days since U.S. forces resumed the naval blockade. As of mid-month, it had said U.S. forces had redirected 138 commercial vessels as part of the effort to ensure strict compliance. Although not used to transport large volumes of either oil, gas or other goods, sea routes across the Caspian, rail routes through Turkmenistan to China and Russia, and air traffic have all been severely curtailed. The U.S. Treasury’s Operation Economic Fury has also disrupted illicit financial transactions, through which Iran managed to access the international financial system – disrupted, but not entirely halted, because Iranians are adept at avoiding U.S. Treasury restrictions, and probably have several fallback means to transact as back doors are identified and closed down. This has all added to the pressure being imposed by the naval blockade, which is doing most of the heavy lifting and by far the most damage to the Iranian regime’s ability to keep on going. But whatever the disruption, and against this backdrop, it must not be forgotten that the Iranian population is used to hardship and is resilient, even though most Iranians dislike their own government and religious rule. Iran still has alternative conduits for trading with the outside world – although not so much in oil and gas, where volumes and a lack of infrastructure make it difficult to find alternative routes out of the country, and where the lack of maritime routes is decisive. Iran enjoys land access across its borders to Pakistan, Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Turkey, and Iraq. But even here, the interagency approach being adopted by the United States means that use of these land routes is now being curtailed. To the east, Turkmenistan, Afghanistan, and Pakistan were never the best of friends with Iran, although Pakistan has said that it intends to increase capacity at its border crossing point at Kuhak; plenty of commerce across the border is smuggling, which does not in any case pass through the designated border control points. The border with Pakistan is particularly tense at present, a consequence of a flare-up of counter-regime insurgency in Iran’s southwestern provinces, spearheaded by Sunni Baluch separatists. None of these countries in reality will move quickly to alleviate delays, wary of U.S. oversight. As a warning of potential consequences, the connection into Turkmenistan and thence to China through the Inche-Burun border crossing in Iran’s north-eastern Golestan Province was disrupted by U.S. bombing of the bridge at Aq Tekeh Khan on July 9. The rail bridge near Aminabad, Isfahan Province, on April 7, 2026 In theory, Azerbaijan could aid Iran by offering increased access through sea, rail and road routes. In theory, Azerbaijan could provide access to Iranian coastal tankers unloading oil products in Baku, at the head of the Cehyan-Tbilisi pipeline. But again, while diplomatic relations are formal and correct, there is no friendship between these two nations to ease open doors. Indeed, Azerbaijan has recently banned the wearing of headscarves in schools, a secularization gesture which will have incensed the Iranians, further soured relationships, and acted as a message to the substantial element of the Azeri minority in Iran’s northern provinces who are at odds with Iran’s religious leadership. A possible trade route to be opened up might be through Armenia’s Zangezur Corridor, sandwiched between two blocks of Azeri territory. But this is a road route only and of limited capacity, and Armenia will not be seeking to please Iran at the expense of its fledgling relationship with NATO and the United States. What used to be a heavily used rail freight route from Tabriz through Jolfa and thence to Armenia and Russia remains inoperative. The land routes linking Iran with Turkey have always been important and heavily used. The Turkish official guide to the old Silk Route border crossing at Bazargan, the busiest crossing point, says that over 200,000 trucks use the checkpoint annually. The checkpoint was expanded to 20 truck lanes earlier this year. Although there are now 1,200 daily crossings, up from 200 a day last year, an Iranian official says that waits at the border have doubled in recent months to about five days, and on October 6, over 4000 trucks were waiting to cross the border. Before getting to Bazargan, trucks from Europe have already often had to wait weeks at the Bulgarian-Turkish border before being able to drive on through Turkey to Bazargan. Aside from two other crossing points at Razi and Serow, the border is marked with a guarded 10-foot-high concrete wall. The sole rail route, from Van in Turkey to Tabriz, mostly carrying passenger traffic, was disabled by bridge strikes during the recent war, but by the end of April some services were back in action. From a trade perspective, the controlled nature of the border would make it easy for the Turkish government to close down – if it wished to succumb to U.S. pressure. The Iranian railway repair crew swings into action on the mainline from Van to Tabriz Finally, there are already signs that the Iraqi government is restricting traffic on its border with Iran, in response to U.S. pressure, and in line with the closing down of air routes. The major crossing at Al Sheeb in Maysan has been closed, and Kurdish politicians expect Mandali to be closed soon as well. Even if the Iraqi Border Crossings Authority does close further customs posts, substantial volumes of goods will continue to be smuggled across what is a very porous border, for the benefit generally of ordinary Iranians rather than the government. The Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al Zaidi has acknowledged he has been requested by Washington to close the border, but will face opposition and disobedience from pro-Iranian politicians. Stay on Top of the Daily Maritime News The maritime news that matters most Get the latest maritime news delivered to your inbox daily. Subscribe Free With the exception of Turkey, where practical difficulties already limit any increased flow of exports and imports, trading through every other Iranian border is either curtailed or restricted. Washington appears to be increasing the pressure on neighboring states to do more. But in any case, only 20% of Iran’s trade has historically traveled across these borders. It is already difficult to switch additional volumes to land routes. Nothing the Iranians can do will be able in any meaningful way to carry more of the 80% of Iranian trade which previously was carried by the merchant marine. Should open warfare resume, Iran has already been weakened by its inability to import and export since the naval blockade was imposed. Iran, as well as global trade generally, remains entirely dependent on shipping, and the impact of the blockade is growing.

sources.text: Romania Blames Russia for Ship Attack Leaving 1 Dead and 3 Missing Romania rescued nine crewmembers, the body of a tenth and three are missing (Interior Ministry) By The Maritime Executive 2026-10-23 12:09:07 Romania is conducting a search and rescue mission after another small cargo ship was attacked in the Black Sea. At the same time, Romania officials reversed earlier calls for investigations and directly blamed Russia for the latest incidents, while the EU and NATO also vowed to increase their support. The Comoros-flagged OBO carrier (Oil-Bulk-Ore carrier) Khoryv (3,280 dwt) issued a distress call on Friday morning, October 23, while it was approximately 13 nautical miles east of Constanta, Romania. The ship was built in 1983 and is 119 meters (390 feet) in length with a crew of 13 aboard. The vessel is listed as being Greek-owned and was sailing from Turkey to the Salina Canal in Romania, which provides access to the Danube. Reports highlight that Ukraine is again relying on this route for shipping after Russia attacks in the Black Sea. Romania’s Interior Ministry said it was informed the vessel had suffered major damage and a fire after a drone strike. The ship later capsized. Another merchant vessel in the area was able to recover nine of the seafarers and the body of one additional person. The crew is reported to consist of 10 Ukrainians and three from Azerbaijan. The Romanian Coast Guard took the nine survivors to shore while a search was launched for three missing crewmembers. The Romanian rescue service joined the search, and a helicopter was on standby, but weather conditions were not allowing aerial involvement. Romanian President Nicusor Dan issued a statement saying, “This attack is a new example of the tragic consequences of Russia's aggression against Ukraine. It is time for Russia to take seriously the peace initiatives of the United States and Europe, to accept the ceasefire proposals, and to end the war.” After the previous attacks, Romanian and Bulgarian officials had refused to identify the source of the attacks, saying it needed investigation. The new prime minister of Romania, only installed in office days ago, also called the attack “unacceptable and constitutes a flagrant violation of international law.” This came after the Ministry of Defense said on Thursday it was accelerating development of maritime surveillance capabilities, including mine countermeasures and effective countermeasures against drones. Reports highlighted that it was at least the seventh attack on a merchant ship in the area between Bulgaria and Romania in the past weeks, with as many as 30 seafarers reported missing or killed. Last week, Romania responded to two attacks near the Sulina Canal, including the attack on the Wine Trade, which left seven crewmembers missing. Stay on Top of the Daily Maritime News The maritime news that matters most Get the latest maritime news delivered to your inbox daily. Subscribe Free “These reckless attacks target innocent lives and openly defy international law,” said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. The European Parliament on Thursday overwhelmingly adopted a resolution (432 votes in favor, 52 against, and 88 abstentions) calling for action. It recommended the EU consider deploying a naval operation in the Black Sea. It was critical of Bulgaria’s “ambiguous handling of the Russian threat,” saying it should take a firmer stance and also stop delaying its participation in NATO’s anti-drone initiative. Furthermore, it also called for NATO to consider a Black Sea initiative while saying EU countries, in cooperation with NATO, needed to support Bulgaria and Romania in early detection and tracking of drones threatening Black Sea shipping. NATO earlier this week resolved to deploy additional assets to the Black Sea.

sources.text: By Thomas Copeland, Mark Poynting and Tom Spencer BBC Verify Published 23 October 2026 An oil spill from a tanker attacked near the Strait of Hormuz is spreading along the United Arab Emirates (UAE) coastline, forcing the closure of some beaches and coastal areas. Satellite images from Monday show the beginnings of the oil spill from a ship matching the location and dimensions of Gem No.2, which was damaged between 9 and 10 October during a record surge of vessel strikes by Iran . The slick of oil had spread more than 35km (22 miles) from the tanker by Wednesday, the satellite imagery showed. UAE authorities said on Thursday that the incident is affecting beaches near the northern city of Umm Al Quwain and verified video from Friday shows the oil washing ashore, colouring the water black. The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Thursday that it "immediately began containment" in order to "limit environmental impacts". Prof Steve Widdicombe, director of Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre in the UAE, told BBC Verify it was "inevitable that there will be an impact", but researchers caution it is too soon to assess extent of the damage. Initially a much smaller oil leak could be seen emerging from the ship on 19 October. But the slick appears to have rapidly spread over two days, according to radar satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify and intelligence firm MAIAR. Oil spills can cause immediate deaths of marine animals and other organisms, for example by physically trapping turtles, smothering the feathers of seabirds or damaging the gills of fish. They can also cause longer-lasting damage, Prof Widdicombe said, if species remain exposed to toxic compounds from the oil which could impact their ability to reproduce. Researchers have cautioned the environmental impact at this stage is very uncertain, as it depends on factors including the volume and type of oil spilled, how quickly it evaporates or breaks down and the effectiveness of the clean-up operation. But the spill does extend towards Siniyah and Khor Al Beidah islands, a globally recognised Key Biodiversity Area containing habitats like corals, seagrasses and saltmarshes, as well as species including green turtles and the critically endangered Halavi guitarfish. The proximity of the spill to this area is the "most concerning environmental angle", according to Eoghan Darbyshire, a scientist at the Conflict and Environment Observatory. Tanker hit 14 days ago BBC Verify analysis of the dimensions and location of the ship indicate they match a crude oil tanker called Gem No.2. Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard reported the Panama-flagged tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile" on 9 October, just north of the town of Al Jazeera Al Hamra, causing a fire on board that was later extinguished. Verified footage first posted on social media on 10 October showed the crew running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rose over the ship. Iranian state media shared footage of a ship matching Gem No.2 which appeared to show the vessel on fire with burning oil spilling into the sea. The ship had been attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an "unauthorized and dangerous route", according to state media. All 22 Indian crew members were rescued, the Indian consulate in Dubai said on 11 October. Gem No.2 is one of a record number of ships that reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz at the start of October . Security experts told BBC Verify this was part of an Iranian effort to assert greater control over the strait, in response to the US military successfully escorting more vessels through the vital shipping lane. Tankers and other commercial vessels have come under attack from both Iranian and US forces in and around the Strait of Hormuz amid the conflict between the two countries. Another major oil slick washed up on the shores of Iran's Qeshm Island in August , which experts said threatened wildlife, protected ecosystems and fishing communities. sources.text: Greek surface and special operations craft validated their new Rafael-made missile systems, while a coordinated submarine torpedo strike sent the decommissioned frigate Bouboulina to the bottom of the Cretan Sea. On Wednesday, October 21, 2026, acceptance firings of SPIKE NLOS and SPIKE ER guided missiles were conducted in the wider northern Cretan Sea area. The firings were attended by Hellenic National Defence General Staff Chief General Dimitrios Choupis, Israeli Navy Commander Vice Admiral Eyal Harel, Hellenic Navy Chief Vice Admiral Dimitrios-Eleftherios Kataras, and Hellenic Fleet Commander Vice Admiral Christos Sasiakos. Greek and Israeli warships in formation in the northern Cretan Sea during the joint live-fire exercise. Hellenic Navy photo. The exercise involved ships from the Hellenic Navy’s Frigate Command, Submarine Command, Fast Attack Craft Command, Surveillance Ship Command, and Underwater Demolition Command, as well as helicopters from the Hellenic Naval Aviation Command and Hellenic Air Force assets. They were joined by two fast attack missile craft from the Israeli Navy, which also conducted undisclosed missile firings during the drills, further enhancing operational interoperability between the two forces. Rafael SPIKE NLOS and SPIKE ER2 missiles were successfully fired from a Machitis -class patrol vessel and a Mark V Special Operations Craft (SOC), respectively. The firings clearly demonstrated the effectiveness and operational value of the newly installed weapon systems. SPIKE NLOS missile launch SPIKE NLOS missile launch SPIKE ER missile launch The decommissioned Hellenic Navy Elli -class (Kortenaer/S-type) frigate Bouboulina (F463) served as the target ship. Following the missile strikes, she was subsequently sunk by an SUT torpedo fired from a Hellenic Navy Papanikolis -class (Type 214HN) submarine. Before her Hellenic Navy service (2001-2013), Bouboulina served with the Royal Netherlands Navy as HNLMS Pieter Florisz (F826). Commissioned in 1983, she was the final Kortenaer -class frigate to be built. The decommissioned Hellenic Navy Elli-class (Korternaer/S-type) frigate Bouboulina (F463) served as the target ship. Hellenic Navy photo. As part of the exercise, the Hellenic Navy Chief and the Israeli Navy Commander held a bilateral meeting aboard the Hellenic Navy Hydra -class (MEKO 200HN) frigate Psara . They exchanged views on matters of mutual interest, focusing on contemporary maritime security challenges, freedom of navigation, and developments across the wider Eastern Mediterranean. Video of the missile firings. Credits to Hellenic Navy. Both navies emphasized the need to further strengthen their cooperation to promote regional stability and security, reaffirming their commitment to expanding partnerships in naval operations, innovation, and new technologies. The exercise took place amid renewed tensions in the Eastern Mediterranean, following the decision by Libya’s eastern-based parliament on October 20 to ratify the controversial 2019 maritime memorandum with Turkey. This development comes amid growing Turkish-Israeli tensions and closer Greek-Israeli defense cooperation, adding to the region’s increasingly complex security environment. SPIKE Missiles in Hellenic Navy Inventory Greece has equipped eight vessels of two different types with Rafael’s SPIKE fire-and-forget missile systems , significantly enhancing their operational capabilities. Machitis-class patrol vessel launching a SPIKE NLOS missile. Hellenic Navy photo. Four Machitis -class patrol vessels are fitted with the Typhoon MLS-NLOS system. Each system is capable of carrying eight SPIKE Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) missiles with a range of 32 km. The sixth-generation electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) multipurpose missile system enables both sea-to-shore fire support and sea-to-sea engagements. The upgrade included the installation of the Typhoon MLS-NLOS launcher, replacing the aft-mounted 40 mm L/70 Breda-Bofors gun fitted on a Type 520R naval mount. Mk V SOC with its Typhoon MLS-ER launcher fitted SPIKE ER missiles visible on the aft deck area. Hellenic Navy photo. The other f our vessels are Mk V Special Operations Craft (SOC) , fitted with the Typhoon MLS-ER system on their stern decks. Integration required significant modifications to the main cabin, mast, and aft deck area. Each craft carries four SPIKE Extended Range (ER) 2 missiles, with a range of 10 km.
